name: Padaleeswarar Temple, Tiruppathiripuliyur
deity: Shiva as Padaleeswarar (Karaiyetreeswarar), with the goddess Periyanayaki
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Nadu Nadu country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century) by Appar and Sambandar; structural temple of the Pallava and medieval Chola tradition, with later additions
dynasty: Pallava and medieval Chola patrons (as traditionally attributed), with later additions
summary: Padaleeswarar is the great Shiva temple of Cuddalore, the Tiruppathiripuliyur of the Tevaram, remembered above all for Appar, who is said to have been cast into the sea bound to a stone and borne safely ashore here by the Lord's grace.

sections.history: Tiruppathiripuliyur, today a part of the town of Cuddalore on the Tamil coast, is one of the Paadal Petra Sthalams of the Nadu Nadu country, sung in the Tevaram by Appar and Sambandar. Its old name joins two memories: the pathiri tree, the temple's sacred tree, and puliyur, the town of the tiger-footed sage Vyaghrapada, and the shrine is counted among the Nava Puliyur temples that tradition ties to Vyaghrapada and Patanjali. Its fame rests above all on Appar, who is said to have been cast into the sea by opponents of his faith and to have come ashore at this place; tradition names the Pallava king Mahendravarman as the one who ordered it. The structural temple is attributed to the Pallava and medieval Chola eras and has been enlarged by later patrons. The details of its building are thinly documented, but worship here has continued across the centuries.
sections.architecture: The temple faces east beneath a five-tiered rajagopuram crowned with seven kalasams, and its spacious enclosure holds the sanctum of Padaleeswarar, where the Lord is worshipped as a linga, and the separate shrine of the goddess Periyanayaki. A small shrine to Arundhava Nayaki, the goddess in her aspect of penance, holds no image: only a plain pedestal marks the spot where she is said to have performed her austerities. The pathiri tree that gives the town its name stands fenced and tended within the precincts. The temple keeps a great car known as Theeruvadaichan, along with a silver chariot and a golden chariot for its processions.
sections.legends: Two traditions gather here. The first is Appar's. The saint is said to have been bound to a boulder and cast into the sea by opponents of his faith. As he sang to the Lord, the stone floated and carried him to the shore at this place, and for this the Lord is also known as Karaiyetreeswarar, the one who brought him to land. The second is the goddess's. Tradition tells that Parvati, in play, covered the eyes of Shiva, and the world fell still; she was told to worship Shiva at a thousand and eight places on earth, and at Tiruppathiripuliyur she completed her penance and became one with the Lord. The bare pedestal of Arundhava Nayaki marks that austerity. The sage Vyaghrapada, whose tiger's feet gave the town half its name, completes the memories the place keeps.
sections.festivals: Padaleeswarar keeps the Shaiva calendar of the Tamil country: Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. The temple's great car and its silver and golden chariots are the vehicles of its festival processions, when the deities are taken out through the streets of the town. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Padaleeswarar suits a slow, attentive visit. Enter beneath the east-facing gopuram, make first for the sanctum of the Lord, and then turn to the shrine of Periyanayaki. Seek out the bare pedestal of Arundhava Nayaki, where an empty seat stands for a devotion beyond images, and pause beside the fenced pathiri tree that gave the town its name. Many visitors come thinking of Appar, the saint carried ashore on a stone, and find in the place a quiet gratitude for being brought safely to the shore. Set within the town of Cuddalore, the temple keeps its calm inside its walls despite the bustle outside.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning from about 6 until noon and again from late afternoon, around 4 until about 8:30 in the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands within Cuddalore town, in the old Tiruppathiripuliyur quarter, and the town is connected by road and rail to Chennai, Puducherry, Chidambaram and the rest of the coast. Local buses and autos reach the temple from the town's bus stand and railway station. Chennai is the principal air gateway, several hours away by road.
